bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in a file called readme located in the home directory. Use this password to log into bandit1 using SSH.
bandit.notes: Initial entry uses the documented starting credentials bandit0/bandit0 (see README); this goal text is bandit1.html's Level Goal, i.e. the bandit0->bandit1 transition.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in a file called – located in the home directory
bandit.notes: Filename is a single dash; needs ./-- or cat < - style referencing to avoid the shell treating it as an option/stdin flag.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in a file called `--spaces in this filename--` located in the home directory
bandit.notes: Filename contains spaces; needs quoting or escaping.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in a hidden file in the **inhere** directory.
bandit.notes: Use ls -a to reveal dotfiles.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the only human-readable file in the **inhere** directory. Tip: if your terminal is messed up, try the "reset" command.
bandit.notes: Use `file *` to identify the ASCII text file among decoys.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in a file somewhere under the inhere directory and has all of the following properties: human-readable, 1033 bytes in size, not executable
bandit.notes: find under inhere with -size 1033c and filter by permissions/file type.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored somewhere on the server and has all of the following properties: owned by user bandit7, owned by group bandit6, 33 bytes in size
bandit.notes: find / -user bandit7 -group bandit6 -size 33c 2>/dev/null, suppressing permission-denied noise.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the file **data.txt** next to the word **millionth**
bandit.notes: grep millionth data.txt

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt and is the only line of text that occurs only once
bandit.notes: sort data.txt | uniq -u

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt in one of the few human-readable strings, preceded by several '=' characters.
bandit.notes: strings data.txt | grep '===' style match on the base64 padding lead-in.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt, which contains base64 encoded data
bandit.notes: base64 -d data.txt

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt, where all lowercase (a-z) and uppercase (A-Z) letters have been rotated by 13 positions
bandit.notes: tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m' < data.txt (ROT13).

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in the file data.txt, which is a hexdump of a file that has been repeatedly compressed. For this level it may be useful to create a directory under /tmp in which you can work. Use mkdir with a hard to guess directory name. Or better, use the command mktemp -d. Then copy the datafile using cp, and rename it using mv (read the manpages!)
bandit.notes: xxd -r to reverse the hexdump, then iteratively `file` + decompress (gzip/bzip2/tar) until a readable password emerges.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in /etc/bandit_pass/bandit14 and can only be read by user bandit14. For this level, you don't get the next password, but you get a private SSH key that can be used to log into the next level. Look at the commands that logged you into previous bandit levels, and find out how to use the key for this level.
bandit.notes: ssh -i sshkey.private bandit14@bandit.labs.overthewire.org -p 2220, then cat /etc/bandit_pass/bandit14.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level can be retrieved by submitting the password of the current level to port 30000 on localhost.
bandit.notes: nc localhost 30000, then paste the bandit14 password.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level can be retrieved by submitting the password of the current level to port 30001 on localhost using SSL/TLS encryption.
bandit.notes: openssl s_client -connect localhost:30001, then paste the password.

bandit.goal: The credentials for the next level can be retrieved by submitting the password of the current level to a port on localhost in the range 31000 to 32000. First find out which of these ports have a server listening on them. Then find out which of those speak SSL/TLS and which don't. There is only 1 server that will give the next credentials, the others will simply send back to you whatever you send to it.
bandit.notes: nmap -p31000-32000 localhost to enumerate, then try openssl s_client on each open SSL port.

bandit.goal: There are 2 files in the homedirectory: passwords.old and passwords.new. The password for the next level is in passwords.new and is the only line that has been changed between passwords.old and passwords.new
bandit.notes: diff passwords.old passwords.new. Note: solving this level modifies bandit18's shell login, which is what the next level (bandit18) is about.

bandit.goal: The password for the next level is stored in a file readme in the homedirectory. Unfortunately, someone has modified .bashrc to log you out when you log in with SSH.
bandit.notes: Bypass .bashrc by running a command directly over ssh, e.g. ssh bandit18@... cat readme.

bandit.goal: To gain access to the next level, you should use the setuid binary in the homedirectory. Execute it without arguments to find out how to use it. The password for this level can be found in the usual place (/etc/bandit_pass), after you have used the setuid binary.
bandit.notes: Page lists no explicit commands section; the setuid binary itself is the tool (run with no args first).

bandit.goal: There is a setuid binary in the homedirectory that does the following: it makes a connection to localhost on the port you specify as a commandline argument. It then reads a line of text from the connection and compares it to the password in the previous level (bandit20). If the password is correct, it will transmit the password for the next level (bandit21).
bandit.notes: Run the setuid binary against a port while a listener (nc -l) on that same port feeds it the current password; needs two concurrent shells/jobs.

bandit.goal: A program is running automatically at regular intervals from cron, the time-based job scheduler. Look in /etc/cron.d/ for the configuration and see what command is being executed.
bandit.notes: cat /etc/cron.d/* to find the script, then read what it does/where it writes.

bandit.goal: A program is running automatically at regular intervals from cron, the time-based job scheduler. Look in /etc/cron.d/ for the configuration and see what command is being executed.
bandit.notes: The referenced script computes something (e.g. a hash of username+date) at runtime; inspect and reproduce its logic manually.

bandit.goal: A program is running automatically at regular intervals from cron, the time-based job scheduler. Look in /etc/cron.d/ for the configuration and see what command is being executed.
bandit.notes: The cron script executes any script dropped in a spool directory; drop your own script there (with correct permissions) to exfiltrate the next password.

bandit.goal: A daemon is listening on port 30002 and will give you the password for bandit25 if given the password for bandit24 and a secret numeric 4-digit pincode. There is no way to retrieve the pincode except by going through all of the 10000 combinations, called brute-forcing. You do not need to create new connections each time
bandit.notes: Script all 10000 4-digit pincodes as newline-delimited input piped into a single nc session rather than reconnecting each time.

bandit.goal: Logging in to bandit26 from bandit25 should be fairly easy… The shell for user bandit26 is not /bin/bash, but something else. Find out what it is, how it works and how to break out of it.
bandit.notes: bandit26's shell is a custom pager (e.g. more/less-style) set via /etc/passwd; shrinking the terminal and using the pager's editor-escape (e.g. 'v' into vi) can break out to a real shell.

bandit.goal: Good job getting a shell! Now hurry and grab the password for bandit27!
bandit.notes: Short follow-on to the bandit25->26 shell escape; just read bandit27's password once you have a working shell as bandit26.

bandit.goal: There is a git repository at ssh://bandit27-git@localhost/home/bandit27-git/repo via the port 2220. The password for the user bandit27-git is the same as for the user bandit27. From your local machine (not the OverTheWire machine!), clone the repository and find the password for the next level. This needs git installed locally on your machine.
bandit.notes: git clone ssh://bandit27-git@bandit.labs.overthewire.org:2220/home/bandit27-git/repo from your own machine, then inspect the checked-out files/history.

bandit.goal: There is a git repository at ssh://bandit28-git@localhost/home/bandit28-git/repo via the port 2220. The password for the user bandit28-git is the same as for the user bandit28. From your local machine (not the OverTheWire machine!), clone the repository and find the password for the next level. This needs git installed locally on your machine.
bandit.notes: Password is not in the current file tree; check git log / older commits for a version that still contains it.

bandit.goal: There is a git repository at ssh://bandit29-git@localhost/home/bandit29-git/repo via the port 2220. The password for the user bandit29-git is the same as for the user bandit29. From your local machine (not the OverTheWire machine!), clone the repository and find the password for the next level. This needs git installed locally on your machine.
bandit.notes: Check other branches (git branch -a / git log --all) in addition to history on the default branch.

bandit.goal: There is a git repository at ssh://bandit30-git@localhost/home/bandit30-git/repo via the port 2220. The password for the user bandit30-git is the same as for the user bandit30. From your local machine (not the OverTheWire machine!), clone the repository and find the password for the next level. This needs git installed locally on your machine.
bandit.notes: Check annotated/lightweight tags (git tag, git show <tag>) in addition to branches and commit history.

bandit.goal: There is a git repository at ssh://bandit31-git@localhost/home/bandit31-git/repo via the port 2220. The password for the user bandit31-git is the same as for the user bandit31. From your local machine (not the OverTheWire machine!), clone the repository and find the password for the next level. This needs git installed locally on your machine.
bandit.notes: Repo likely has a .gitignore blocking a specific filename; force-add and commit/push that exact file (per the repo's README instructions) to reveal the password.

bandit.goal: After all this `git` stuff, it's time for another escape. Good luck!
bandit.notes: Login shell is an uppercase-only wrapper (e.g. everything piped through tr a-z A-Z); spawn a real shell using a control operator that survives uppercasing, e.g. $0 or /bin/sh via a command substitution.

bandit.goal: This is the final account in the Bandit wargame. There is no bandit34 and no further banditN.html page describing another password to find; reaching bandit33 completes Bandit.
bandit.notes: End of Bandit. (This goal text is our own terminal-state note, not verbatim OTW page text, since no such page exists.)

krypton.goal: The first level is easy. The following string encodes the password using Base64: S1JZUFRPTklTR1JFQVQ=
krypton.notes: There is no real SSH account krypton0; this is a browser-only intro puzzle. Decoding the Base64 string yields KRYPTONISGREAT, the documented starting password for krypton1.

krypton.goal: The password for level 2 is in the file 'krypton2'. It is 'encrypted' using a simple rotation. It is also in non-standard ciphertext format. When using alpha characters for cipher text it is normal to group the letters into 5 letter clusters, regardless of word boundaries. This helps obfuscate any patterns. This file has kept the plain text word boundaries and carried them to the cipher text. Enjoy!
krypton.notes: Simple Caesar/rotation cipher; preserved word boundaries make short words (e.g. 'a', 'the') easy anchors for finding the shift. Page has no dedicated Commands list.

krypton.goal: ROT13 is a simple substitution cipher. This level contains an old form of cipher called a 'Caesar Cipher'. A Caesar cipher shifts the alphabet by a set number. The password for level 3 is in the file krypton3. It is in 5 letter group ciphertext. It is encrypted with a Caesar Cipher. You do not have direct access to the key, however you do have access to a program that will encrypt anything you wish to give it using the key. If you think logically, this is completely easy. One shot can solve it!
krypton.notes: A setuid 'encrypt' oracle (using keyfile.dat) lets you encrypt chosen plaintext with the same key as krypton3's ciphertext, revealing the shift in one query (chosen-plaintext attack).

krypton.goal: Well done. You've moved past an easy substitution cipher. The main weakness of a simple substitution cipher is repeated use of a simple key. In the previous exercise you were able to introduce arbitrary plaintext to expose the key. In this example, the cipher mechanism is not available to you, the attacker. However, you have been lucky. You have intercepted more than one message. The password to the next level is found in the file 'krypton4'. You have also found 3 other files. (found1, found2, found3) You know the following important details: The message plaintexts are in American English (*** very important) - They were produced from the same key (*** even better!)
krypton.notes: No encryption oracle this time; use the found1/found2/found3 known-plaintext messages (all under the same key) to recover the key and decrypt krypton4.

krypton.goal: This level is a Vigenère Cipher. You have intercepted two longer, english language messages (American English). You also have a key piece of information. You know the key length! For this exercise, the key length is 6.
krypton.notes: Known key length (6) lets you split ciphertext into 6 interleaved Caesar-cipher streams and solve each with frequency analysis.

krypton.goal: FA can break a known key length as well. Lets try one last polyalphabetic cipher, but this time the key length is unknown. Note: the text is writen in American English
krypton.notes: Key length must first be recovered (e.g. Kasiski examination / index of coincidence) before per-column frequency analysis (FA) can solve the Vigenère cipher.

krypton.goal: A stream cipher attempts to create an on-the-fly 'random' keystream to encrypt the incoming plaintext one byte at a time. The password for krypton7 is encrypted using the encrypt6 binary, which relies on a weak random number generator. This is a known-ciphertext style attack where you can introduce plaintext of your choice; files provided include plain1, key1, cipher1, keyfile, HINT1 and HINT2. Public analysis tools such as cryptool may help; this challenge is not simple.
krypton.notes: Exploit the weak PRNG behind encrypt6 (e.g. recover/predict its keystream from known plaintext/ciphertext pairs) to decrypt krypton7's password. krypton7 is the final account in the Krypton wargame; this dataset only covers levels 0-6 as requested, so krypton7.html was not fetched.
